title: Both ends of three translation features
takeaway: Projecting a transcoder feature's encoder and decoder directions separately through the J-lens makes the feature's input-to-output map readable without running the model on any data. In all three cases shown, the encoder side reads a concept expressed across many languages together with common French words, and the decoder side writes the opening token of the French word for that concept.
walkthrough:
The item renders as a live panel rather than a static plot. Three columns sit side by side, one per [[transcoder]] feature, headed Water → eau, Love → amour and Game → jeu. Each column splits into an Encoder box and a Decoder box, and each box lists ten vocabulary tokens.

A transcoder approximates one MLP layer with a sparsely activating hidden layer. Each of its features owns two directions in the [[residual-stream]]. The encoder direction determines what content switches the feature on. The decoder direction is what the feature writes back when it fires.

### How to read it

Both directions are ordinary vectors, so both can be pushed through the lens. The box headers state the composition used: Encoder · J · W$_U$ and Decoder · J · W$_U$. The direction is multiplied by the averaged Jacobian $J$ that defines the [[jacobian-lens]], then by the unembedding matrix $W_U$, which scores every token in the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. Sorting those scores gives the ranking. This is the weight-side [[j-lens-readout]]: [[weight-vocabulary-projection]], one application of [[component-interpretation]].

The small number beside a token is its rank in that full ordering, so 1 is the top-scoring token. Colour marks a category. Blue is a token naming the concept in some language, magenta a common French word, teal the French target word or a fragment of it, and gray a token left uncategorised.

The decoder lists run 1 through 10 with no gaps. The encoder lists do not: the water encoder shows ranks 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8, then jumps to 30, 39, 41 and 50. Those rows are selected entries, not an unbroken top of the list. The prose also names tokens absent from the rows shown, such as aigua for water.

### What it shows

Each encoder reads two things at once. It reads the concept across languages — water, 水, água, agua and вод — and separately reads common French words, avec, école, une and dans, which say nothing about water. The same split appears for love and for game.

Each decoder writes the beginning of the French word. The water decoder is led by eau and by fragments starting ea. The love decoder writes am, the opening of amour, in Latin, Cyrillic and Korean script. The game decoder writes j, the opening of jeu, in Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, Japanese and Devanagari script.

Taken together the two sides name a function: concept plus French context in, first token of the French translation out. The language-agnostic half of each encoder is the paper's [[shared-multilingual-representation]] appearing in weights rather than in activations.

terms.definition: A dictionary-learning variant trained to reproduce an MLP layer's input-to-output map through a sparsely activating hidden layer. Each hidden unit is a feature with its own encoder and decoder direction, which is what lets the two sides be read separately here.

The feature's input direction: the residual-stream direction whose dot product with the incoming activation decides whether the feature switches on. The left box in each column reads this direction through the lens.
The feature's output direction: the vector the feature adds back to the residual stream, scaled by its activation. The right box in each column reads this direction through the lens.

The averaged Jacobian at the heart of the J-lens — the linear map, estimated by averaging per-input Jacobians over a corpus, from a residual-stream perturbation to its effect on the model's output logits. Multiplying a direction by $J$ asks what that direction would push the model to say.
The model's unembedding matrix, which turns a final-layer vector into one score per vocabulary token. It is the last step of the composition printed in each box header.

terms.term: Encoder · J · W$_U$ / Decoder · J · W$_U$
terms.definition: The box headers, naming the exact quantity ranked below them: take the feature direction, push it through the averaged Jacobian, then through the unembedding. No forward pass on real text is involved, which is why the paper calls this a data-free reading.
The paper's technique for reading a residual-stream direction as a distribution over words the model could say about it. Applied here to static weight directions rather than to activations.
The label running down the left edge of the panel. It states that the vertical axis of each list is position in the ranking, best at the top, rather than a score.

For each token, its position when the whole tokenizer vocabulary is sorted by the score from that composition. Rank 1 is the highest-scoring token in the vocabulary; the caption states plainly that the numbers are ranks.
The title of the first column. It names the feature by the English concept its encoder reads and the French word its decoder starts to write.
The title of the second column, read the same way: a love-concept encoder paired with a decoder that opens the French word amour.
The title of the third column: a game-concept encoder paired with a decoder that opens the French word jeu.
The colour given to a token that names the column's concept in some language, whatever the script. It marks the language-agnostic half of what the encoder reads.

The colour given to a common French word that carries no information about the concept — function words and everyday nouns. Its presence in the encoder readout is what tells the reader the feature is conditioned on French, not just on the concept.
The colour given to the French word for the concept or to a fragment that opens it. The figure's caption refers to this category as the French word.
Tokens the authors did not assign to any of the three categories, such as eat, wash, ear and a. They appear high in some decoder lists and are not claimed to support the interpretation.
The character the widget prints where a token contains a leading or trailing space. It distinguishes a whole-word token such as ⍽eau⍽ from a word-initial fragment such as ⍽am.

The concept tokens in the first feature's encoder readout: water in English, Chinese, Portuguese, Spanish and Russian. Together they are the evidence that the encoder reads a concept rather than a string.
The French word for water. It appears in the first feature's encoder readout at rank 7 and dominates its decoder readout at rank 1.

terms.term: avec, école, une, dans, qui, à, elle, pour
terms.definition: The common French tokens appearing in the encoder readouts of all three features: with, school, a, in, who, to, she, for. None of them relates to water, love or games; the paper reads them as the French-context condition on the feature.

terms.term: ea, EA, ean, eat, ear, wash, E
terms.definition: The remaining tokens in the water decoder's top ten. The teal ones (ea, EA, ean) are fragments that open eau or eau-like French spellings; eat, ear, wash and E are uncategorised near-misses on the same letters or on the water theme.

The concept tokens in the second feature's encoder readout: love in English, Spanish or Portuguese, a South Slavic stem, and a German stem. The paper's prose also lists romance and marriage, which are not among the ten rows displayed.

terms.term: am, Am, ам, а, ам (Cyrillic), 아, a
terms.definition: The second feature's decoder readout: the fragment am in Latin, Cyrillic and Korean script, plus bare a. The paper reads these as the opening of amour written in whatever script the vocabulary offers.

terms.term: иг, game, ját, 游, spiel, 게, jou
terms.definition: The concept tokens in the third feature's encoder readout: game or play stems in Russian, English, Hungarian, Chinese, German, Korean and French. The Russian stem иг outranks the English game.

terms.term: j, ј, J, дж, ج, ジ, ज
terms.definition: The third feature's decoder readout: the letter j and its nearest equivalents in Cyrillic, Arabic, Japanese katakana and Devanagari. The paper reads them as the start of jeu.

Tokens the surrounding prose names as present in these encoder readouts — aigua is Catalan for water — but which do not appear among the ten rows the panel displays. The displayed rows are a selection, not the complete readout.

The paper's finding that a multilingual model routes some computation through a representation that is not tied to any one language. Here it shows up in a weight direction: one encoder reads the same concept written five different ways.

numbers.meaning: The number of transcoder features shown, one per column. All three are chosen as translation features, so the panel is an illustration of a pattern rather than a survey of how common it is.
The number of token rows in each of the six boxes. Ten is a display choice; the underlying ranking covers the whole vocabulary.
The best rank, meaning the token that scores highest in the whole vocabulary for that composition. Every decoder box here is headed by a token the paper counts as on-target: eau, am and j.

The top block of the water encoder: water (1), 水 (3), água (5), agua (6), eau (7), вод (8). Six of the eight highest-ranked slots shown are the same concept in different languages, which is the figure's main evidence that the encoder is concept-driven.
Ranks absent from the water encoder list. Their absence shows that the displayed rows are selected entries rather than an unbroken top ten, so nothing can be concluded about what sits in the gaps.

The ranks of avec, école, une and dans in the water encoder. They sit well below the concept tokens but still inside the top fifty of a vocabulary of tens of thousands, which the paper treats as a real French-context signal rather than noise.
A contiguous top ten: eau, eau, eat, ea, wash, ear, E, E, EA, ean. Four rows are teal French-target fragments and the rest are uncategorised, so the decoder's list is less clean than the encoder's.

The concept ranks in the love encoder: love (1), amor (3), ljub (10) and lieb (31). The German stem lieb falls below several French function words, which shows the two categories interleave rather than separating into blocks.
The ranks of the French context tokens qui, dans, avec, à, elle and pour in the love encoder. They begin higher than in the water encoder, at 21 rather than 30.
A contiguous top ten: am, a, ам, Am, am, а, Am, 아, a, ам. Seven rows are the am fragment in some script or case; the two bare a rows are uncategorised.
The concept ranks in the game encoder: иг (1), game (2), ját (6), 游 (7), spiel (13), 게 (18), jou (36). The Russian stem outranks the English word, so the readout is not simply English-first.
The ranks of dans, à and pour in the game encoder. This is the weakest of the three French-context signals, the first such token arriving only at rank 42.
A contiguous top ten: j, j, ј, дж, ج, J, ジ, ज, ج, J. Every row is the j sound or letter in some script, making this the sharpest of the three decoder readouts.
